notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: He opened by saying he was job hunting, for associate product manager or product analyst roles. Composer hired him as a UX developer anyway, on the strength of what he had already built.

notes.label: Old career, in the experience list
notes.note: His year as a product analyst at Soapbox is one line in the experience list, not a story. Three of the six career switchers in the set showed their old field on the homepage, and none of them led with it.

notes.label: Building in public
notes.note: A project that isn't finished yet, with a link to his build journal. Seven of the ten published writing beyond their case studies.

notes.label: Project card, no case study
notes.note: One paragraph per project, with the demo and code linked. None of the three design engineers in the set had case studies. They were hired on things they had shipped.

notes.label: A craft outside design
notes.note: Photography gets its own section, and he backs it up: one of his photos is a default wallpaper on every Google Pixel.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: A greeting aimed at design and research readers, with no job title. She's the only one of the seven product designers in the set who didn't say "designer" on her first screen.

notes.label: A specific angle
notes.note: She names her angle: making complex decisions simple. Four of the ten named an audience or theme like this.

notes.label: Old career, just below the fold
notes.note: Her psychology background comes right after the first screen, framed as a strength: turning research insights into solutions. Hers is the background closest to mine in the set.

notes.label: Work, three screens down
notes.note: Her work starts after the skills list: three case studies and a writing sample. Four of the ten showed work on the first screen, so where the work goes is still an open question for me.

notes.label: Someone else's voice
notes.note: Quotes from two people she has worked with, right on the homepage. Four of the ten used someone else's voice, and she and Leo put it on the homepage.

notes.label: Facts block
notes.note: Framework, timeline, role and tools, before anything else. All five readable case studies in the set opened with a block like this, and hers says up front that it was a bootcamp capstone.

notes.label: Her old field, turned into a niche
notes.note: She taught special education, and her capstone designs for people with motor disabilities. Voiceitt, which builds speech technology for people with disabilities, hired her as its only designer.

notes.label: A user's voice
notes.note: A quote from a potential user who uses a wheelchair, near the top of the case study. Four of the ten used someone else's voice, and two of them put it inside a case study.

notes.label: Research with real people
notes.note: Five in-person interviews with wheelchair users. Every readable case study in the set showed research or testing with real participants.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: One sentence that nods to her old career in marine biology: she loves "diving beneath the surface" of other people's worlds. Her homepage is about 215 words, and the depth is in the case studies.

notes.label: Old career, on About
notes.note: The full story of her switch from marine biology and teaching is one click away on her About page, not on the homepage.

notes.label: Case studies that go deep
notes.note: Each card opens a full case study. Hers run 2,600 to 3,400 words, the longest in the set.

notes.label: Lighter work, labeled
notes.note: One project says "Preview work" instead of "Read case study," so it's clear it isn't a full case study. Nobody in the set mixed smaller work in with case studies unmarked.

notes.label: Real client work, first
notes.note: Her one real client project leads her portfolio, ahead of three concept projects. Everyone in the set who had real work led with it.

notes.label: Facts block
notes.note: Client, role and duration before anything else. All five readable case studies in the set opened with a block like this.

notes.label: The problem, up front
notes.note: The challenge comes right after the facts: the studio had grown through word-of-mouth referrals. All five readable case studies stated the problem in the opening.

notes.label: Process, in order
notes.note: The case study walks through the design process in order, starting with research. All five readable case studies were structured this way.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: "Hey, you." A direct, warm opener. Seven of the ten had a clear personal voice like this.

notes.label: Role, angle and a playlist
notes.note: She names the role and an angle, humanizing tech, then links a playlist. The first two say what she does, and the playlist says something about who she is.

notes.label: A concept, well timed
notes.note: Her first case study is a concept: a Clubhouse redesign she wrote while everyone was talking about Clubhouse. Five of the seven product designers in the set included a concept project.

notes.label: Four case studies
notes.note: Four case studies on the homepage, with visual experiments kept on a separate Play page. Every product designer in the set showed three to five.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: His role first, then one line on what he cares about. Six of the seven product designers said "designer" on their first screen.

notes.label: Play, in the nav
notes.note: Experiments live on a separate Play page, one click away. Three of the seven product designers had one.

notes.label: Facts on every card
notes.note: Each case study card carries a summary, his role, his contributions and the timeline, so you know what he did before you click.

notes.label: Internship work, in motion
notes.note: His Dropbox internship projects show the interactions in video, with up to 10 videos per case study. Interaction and flows is 19% of portfolio asks in the job posts.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: A short line in the third person, then where he works now: leading design at Corgi, previously at Snapchat.

notes.label: Titles that say what changed
notes.note: Each case study is titled by what the work did, like "Scaling student housing with a cohesive design system," with the client and year underneath.

notes.label: A competition project
notes.note: A design-a-thon project sits alongside client work, labeled as a finalist. Five of the seven product designers in the set included a concept or competition project.

notes.label: Someone else's voice
notes.note: "The receipts": quotes from a design engineer at Wealthsimple and a principal product designer at 1Password, right on the homepage. Four of the ten used someone else's voice.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: No job title, just an angle: prototyping digital environments inspired by play. Two of the three design engineers in the set skipped the role line.

notes.label: Experiments, not case studies
notes.note: Small experiments in place of case studies. None of the three design engineers had case studies. They were hired on working things.

notes.label: Notes on how she made them
notes.note: Process notes of 670 to 890 words on what she learned making each thing. Seven of the ten published writing beyond their case studies.

notes.label: AI, before the AI job
notes.note: Several of her experiments prototype language model interactions. Her first design engineering job was at an AI company, Hume AI.

notes.label: Leads with
notes.note: Just her name and "Design Engineer." She's the one design engineer in the set who named the role on her first screen.

notes.label: One feed, two audiences
notes.note: Her posts filter into Product Design and Engineering, so each kind of reviewer can go straight to their half.

notes.label: The internship that became the job
notes.note: Her posts run 16 to 104 words, mostly images, including her Viam internship. Viam hired her as a product designer after it.

notes.label: A timeline
notes.note: A timeline of key life and work events closes the page.
